question.en: A React Native list of hundreds of rows scrolls poorly. What would you inspect and change first?

selectedId changes in the parent, data does not, and half the rows in the FlatList never re-render to show the new selection. The team proposes forcing it with keyExtractor={(item) => item.id + '-' + selectedId}. Why is that wrong, and what is the right fix?

answer.en: FlatList is a PureComponent, so it only re-renders when its props change; a value that affects rows but lives outside data must arrive as a changed prop, which is exactly what extraData is for: pass extraData={selectedId}. Baking selection into the key is worse than the bug. Keys identify items across renders, so changing them remounts the affected rows, discarding row state and animations and breaking identity-based optimizations.

question.en: You add getItemLayout to skip measurement, and scrolling gets worse: fast scrolls land on the wrong rows and content overlaps. What happened?

answer.en: getItemLayout is only valid when row geometry is truly uniform. If any row can be taller than the declared length, for example text that wraps to extra lines, every offset after it is wrong: the list scrolls to computed positions that no longer match reality, and it skipped the measurement that would have corrected it. Either guarantee fixed heights by constraining row content, or remove getItemLayout and let the list measure.

question.en: What is React Native's basic rendering model, and how should a developer think about platform differences?
Design asks for the iOS and Android apps to be pixel-identical, citing brand consistency. How do you respond as the engineer responsible for the React Native app?

answer.en: Push back on identical pixels, not on consistency. The goal is a consistent product contract: the same capabilities, flows, and quality, implemented in ways that respect each platform. Keyboard behavior, permissions, navigation, accessibility, and the system back button all differ by platform, and forcing them to match one platform's conventions usually degrades the app on the other. Isolate the genuine differences behind platform APIs, platform-specific files, or small adapter components so the shared core stays clean.

question.en: A codebase has Platform.OS === 'ios' checks scattered through 30 components and several business-logic modules. Refactoring is labeled nice to have. Why is it actually a correctness and velocity problem?

answer.en: Every scattered check multiplies the platform matrix the team must test and turns platform differences into invisible branches of business logic. The fix is a small platform seam: platform-specific files, Platform.select for values, and adapter components that expose one interface and hide the split. Platform behavior is then validated once at the seam instead of being rediscovered in every feature.

question.en: What changed in React Native's New Architecture, and what would you verify before migrating a production app?

answer.en: The New Architecture replaces the asynchronous bridge with JSI-based JavaScript/native interop, adds the Fabric renderer, and supports concurrent React features. JSI lets JavaScript and C++ hold references and invoke methods without the old serialization cost; Fabric enables capabilities such as synchronous layout access. Those capabilities do not automatically make every app faster: the official guidance warns that an app may need refactoring and that serialization may not have been its bottleneck. Before migration, inventory native dependencies and verify their New Architecture compatibility, test layout measurement, lists, gestures, startup, memory, and accessibility on real devices, and compare production-like profiles. Roll out gradually with crash and performance telemetry, keeping a tested fallback only if the chosen React Native release supports it.

question.en: Leadership approved the New Architecture migration because removing the bridge makes the app faster. Six weeks after migrating, startup and scroll metrics are flat. Explain what the team misunderstood.

answer.en: The New Architecture replaces asynchronous bridge serialization with JSI-based interop and adds Fabric, which enables capabilities such as synchronous layout access. Those are capabilities, not automatic speedups: the official guidance warns that an app may need refactoring to benefit and that serialization may never have been the app's bottleneck. If the pre-migration profile showed the time going elsewhere, for example JS execution or native rendering, removing serialization cannot move those numbers.

question.en: The migration plan says: if New Architecture causes regressions, we will flip back to the old architecture. What is fragile about that rollback plan?

answer.en: It assumes the old architecture is still available on the React Native release you ship. The safe wording is a tested fallback only if the chosen release supports it. On releases where the old architecture is gone, there is nothing to flip back to, so the plan must instead be gradual rollout with crash and performance telemetry, and a halt procedure that stops the rollout rather than reverting the architecture.

question.en: When would you choose Expo tooling over a React Native project managed directly with native tooling?

answer.en: Treat this as a workflow choice, not a permanent split between two frameworks: an Expo app is still a React Native app, and Expo tools can be adopted independently. Expo provides app configuration, development builds, prebuild or Continuous Native Generation, and optional hosted EAS services for building, submitting, and updating. It is a strong default when the team values convention, repeatable native configuration, and a managed build pipeline. Direct native project ownership can be appropriate when the organization needs bespoke Gradle or Xcode integration, unusual native modules, or native changes that it wants to review and maintain directly. Expo Go is a limited playground, not the production development environment; use a development build when native libraries or production-like behavior matter. Decide from native requirements and operational constraints, then document the boundary.

question.en: The team hit a wall: the app needs a native library, and Expo Go cannot load it. The proposal on the table is to eject to bare React Native. What is usually the better move, and why?

answer.en: Usually the better move is a development build: a build of your own project that includes the native libraries, produced through Expo's app configuration and prebuild pipeline. Expo Go is a limited playground, not the production development environment, so its limits are the wall, not Expo itself. Ejecting to direct native ownership is justified by bespoke Gradle or Xcode integration or unusual native modules, not by the mere need for a native library.

question.en: In an Expo project using Continuous Native Generation, a developer hand-edits the generated Xcode project to add a build setting. What happens to that edit, and where should the change live instead?

answer.en: The native projects are generated, so a hand edit can be overwritten the next time the native projects are regenerated. The change belongs in the app configuration layer that drives generation, so the native project stays reproducible from source. If the setting cannot be expressed there, that is the signal to evaluate whether this specific customization justifies direct native ownership of the project.

question.en: What release-readiness concerns must a cross-platform team cover before submitting a mobile app to Apple and Google Play?

answer.en: Release readiness is more than producing two binaries. Test the submitted builds on devices, verify that backend services and login or demo access are available for review, and make metadata, screenshots, privacy disclosures, permissions, and in-app purchase behavior accurate. Apple says submissions must be complete and functional, uses only public APIs, and must work on IPv6-only networks; it also expects review notes and access to account-based features. Google Play uses Android App Bundles to generate device-optimized APKs, requires signing, and applies target API and account-specific testing requirements. Establish a release checklist with reproducible builds, signing ownership, staged or beta distribution, crash monitoring, rollback or halt procedures, and a named owner for policy changes. Recheck current store rules for every release because they change.

question.en: The app works perfectly on the office network, but Apple review rejects it for failing to load content. The submission is complete and uses only public APIs. What environmental condition did testing miss?

answer.en: Apple requires submissions to work on IPv6-only networks. A backend or dependency that still assumes IPv4 can pass every internal test on a dual-stack office network and fail review. Reproduce it by testing on an IPv6-only network before submitting, and recheck the current App Review guidelines for every release because the rules change.

question.en: The release plan uploads a single universal APK to Google Play. What is wrong with that submission format?

answer.en: Google Play uses Android App Bundles: you upload the signed bundle and Play generates device-optimized APKs from it. A universal APK ships every density and architecture to every device, which bloats the download, and it is not the submission format Play's current requirements expect. Bundle, sign, and let Play do the per-device splitting.
